questions.question_text: For the curve $y=4^x$, what is the behaviour as $x\to-\infty$?

options.why: confused approaching the horizontal asymptote with negative infinite decay
gave the behaviour as $x\to\infty$ instead of $x\to-\infty$
confused the base of the exponential with a horizontal asymptote
treated the negative index as growth instead of exponential decay
assumed a negative index causes negative values rather than small positive fractions
used the negative base number instead of the asymptote $y=0$

questions.question_text: For $y=-3^x$, which pair describes the end behaviour as $x\to\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$?

options.why: ignored the negative coefficient which reflects the curve across the $x$-axis
swapped the growing end with the decaying end
assumed the curve tends to negative infinity at both ends

questions.solution_text:
The negative sign reflects $y=3^x$ across the $x$-axis.
As $x\to\infty$, $3^x\to\infty$, so $y\to-\infty$.
As $x\to-\infty$, $3^x\to0$, so $y\to0$.

questions.question_text: For the exponential function $y=3(2^x)-7$, what are the limits as $x\to\infty$ and as $x\to-\infty$?

options.why: forgot that the vertical shift $-7$ moves the horizontal asymptote to $y=-7$
swapped the infinite growth end with the asymptotic end
subtracted $3$ from $-7$ or evaluated at $x=0$ instead of taking the limit as $x\to-\infty$

questions.question_text: Why does the graph of $y=2(5^x)+4$ never take any value less than or equal to $4$?

options.text: Because $5^x > 0$ for all real $x$, which ensures $2(5^x)+4 > 4$.
Because as $x\to-\infty$, $5^x\to0$, so the curve attains its minimum value at $y=4$.
options.why: falsely claims that the curve reaches its horizontal asymptote at $y=4$ rather than strictly approaching it from above

options.text: Because the $y$-intercept is $(0,6)$, which is strictly greater than $4$.
options.why: relies on the value at $x=0$ rather than the universal positivity of exponential powers

options.text: Because $2(5^x)$ increases towards positive infinity in both directions.
options.why: falsely asserts that the exponential function grows infinitely large as $x\to-\infty$

questions.solution_text:
For all real $x$, $5^x > 0$.
$2(5^x) > 0$
$2(5^x)+4 > 4$
Therefore $y$ is strictly greater than $4$ for every real number $x$.

questions.question_text:
An exponential curve $y=k(2^x)+c$ has a horizontal asymptote of $y=-3$ as $x\to-\infty$ and passes through $(0,5)$.
What is the equation of the curve, and what is its limit as $x\to\infty$?

options.why: used the $y$-intercept value $5$ directly as $k$ without adding the vertical shift offset
used $+3$ instead of $-3$ for the horizontal asymptote constant $c$
subtracted $3$ from $5$ instead of setting $k+(-3)=5$ to find $k=8$

questions.solution_text:
Horizontal asymptote is $y=c = -3$.
At $(0,5)$:
$5 = k(2^0)+c$
$5 = k-3$
$k = 8$
Equation: $y=8(2^x)-3$
As $x\to\infty$, $2^x\to\infty$, so $y\to\infty$.
